name: Base rate fallacy
statement: Told that a test with a 5% false-positive rate flags a disease one person in a thousand has, most people answer 95% rather than about 2%.
meaning: Bayes's rule says a posterior probability depends on three things: how common the condition is, how often the test catches it, and how often the test fires on people who do not have it. The complaint is that people attend to the second and third and drop the first. Two families of demonstration sit under the one name and they are not the same experiment. In the diagnosis family the numbers are all given, the answer is a calculation, and the finding is a percentage of people who get it wrong. In the personality-sketch family a description is drawn from a stated mix of two professions, and the finding is that judgments barely move when the mix is reversed. That second family is the property of the representativeness heuristic, which supplies the mechanism: a description that sounds like an engineer is treated as evidence of an engineer whatever the panel contained. This entry follows the first family, where the stakes are diagnostic tests, screening programmes and forensic evidence.

origin.note: "On the Psychology of Prediction" reported the engineer-lawyer problem, in which descriptions were said to be drawn at random from a panel of either 30 engineers and 70 lawyers or 70 engineers and 30 lawyers. The 1973 paper could not be opened during this check. Its figures are taken from Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank, who report that mean judgments were 5% higher on the probability scale in the group given the higher engineer base rate, and that the median judgment for the deliberately uninformative description of Dick was .50 in both groups. The medical version arrived separately and is the one that travels.

evidence: The mammography problem is the canonical case. A woman of forty has a 1% chance of breast cancer, the test catches 80% of cancers, and it fires on 9.6% of women without one. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage state the Bayesian answer as 7.8%, and report that Eddy's 1982 chapter found 95 of 100 physicians putting it between 70% and 80%. Eddy's chapter was not opened during this check, so that figure reaches this page at one remove. Casscells, Schoenberger and Graboys ran a shorter version at Harvard Medical School teaching hospitals: a disease with a prevalence of 1 in 1,000, a false-positive rate of 5%, and a positive result. Their 1978 report is a letter of three pages and could not be opened either. Manrai and colleagues, who reproduce the question, give 11 of 60 correct and 27 answering 95%. Gigerenzer and colleagues put the same study's success rate at 18%. Bar-Hillel's cab problem made the point without medicine. Fifty-two people were told 85% of a city's cabs are blue and a witness who is right about 80% of the time reported green. Bayes gives 41%, the median answer was 80%, and about 10% of respondents came near 41%.

replication.headline: The diagnostic version repeats almost exactly across four decades, rewriting it as counts of people roughly triples the number of correct answers, and the benefit lands hardest on the people who were already numerate.
replication.detail: Manrai, Bhatia, Strymish, Kohane and Jain put the Casscells question to 61 people at a Boston-area hospital, 24 of them attending physicians. Fourteen (23%) gave the correct 2%, 27 (44%) said 95%, and the median answer was 66%, which the authors note is 33 times the true value. Stengård, Juslin, Hahn and van den Berg ran the classic wording on 100 online participants as a control: 9% were correct, and the modal answer was again 95%. Gigerenzer and colleagues report a training session in 2007 at which 160 gynaecologists were given a 1% prevalence, a 90% sensitivity and a 9% false-positive rate and four answer options an order of magnitude apart. Estimates ranged from 1% to 90%, the majority chose 81% or 90%, and 21% picked the correct 1 in 10, which the authors note is below chance for a four-option question. After the same numbers were retaught as natural frequencies, 87% got it right. The format effect is the most-repeated result here. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage gave 60 paid students at the University of Salzburg 15 inference problems, each in two of four versions, scoring an answer as Bayesian only when both the process and the number were right. Probability wording produced 16% Bayesian solutions with the standard menu and 28% with the short menu. The same information written as counts produced 46% and 50%. McDowell and Jacobs pooled 226 performance estimates from 35 articles; Weber, Binder and Krauss quote them as putting performance at 24% for natural frequencies against 4% for probabilities. Bramwell, West and Salmon tested a Down's syndrome screening question on 43 pregnant women, 40 companions, 42 midwives and 41 obstetricians. Twenty-four of 166 were right. Frequencies beat percentages, 24% against 6% (χ² = 10.4, df = 1, P = 0.001), and 86% of responses were still wrong. Stengård and colleagues found the same direction and a smaller gap across 45 varied problems: mean absolute error was 18.0 with natural frequencies against 23.2 with normalised formats, and 46 of 91 participants were classified as Bayesian against 31 of 91. The personality-sketch version behaves differently. Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank re-ran the engineer-lawyer problem with 24 people per cell of a two-by-two design. Merely asserting random sampling gave a base-rate effect of 9.8 points, about twice the original 5%. Letting participants draw the description from an urn themselves lifted it to 17.3 points. Toubia and colleagues put the problem to a representative US sample of 2,058 people across four waves. It was the only between-subject classic in their battery that failed: mean judgments were 52.17% in the 30-engineer condition and 68.01% in the 70-engineer condition (t = -15.78, p < .01), repeated in wave four at 52.39% and 70.71%.

study.cite: Manrai, A. K., Bhatia, G., Strymish, J., Kohane, I. S., & Jain, S. H. (2014). Medicine's uncomfortable relationship with math: Calculating positive predictive value. JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(6), 991-993.

limits: No multi-site preregistered replication of base-rate neglect was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, the BMJ, bioRxiv, arXiv and the journals themselves turned up no Many Labs or Registered Replication Report entry for either paradigm, so the record is a meta-analysis, one large representative survey, and single-laboratory experiments. Three originals could not be opened: Kahneman and Tversky's 1973 paper, Eddy's 1982 book chapter and the 1978 Casscells letter. Their numbers here come from Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank, from Gigerenzer and Hoffrage, and from Manrai and colleagues, all of whom reproduce them. Operskalski and Barbey's 2016 review in Science sits behind a paywall and was not read, so nothing is quoted from it. The famous physician figures also rest on small samples: 60 people in 1978, 100 in Eddy's chapter, 61 in the 2014 repeat. The effect is measured almost entirely in one corner of the problem space. Stengård and colleagues make the point directly: the standard problems use base rates near zero, near-perfect hit rates and low false-alarm rates, where a Bayesian answer and base-rate neglect are far apart. Across five base rates from 0.1 to 0.9 they found the pattern generalises, but with a bimodal split, one group of participants ignoring the base rate almost entirely and another using it almost fully. A group average of partial neglect can describe a population in which nobody partially neglects anything.
misreadings: The strongest reading, that people ignore base rates, is the one the evidence does not carry. Koehler's review concluded that base rates are almost always used, and that how much depends on task structure and representation. Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank make the same case with a manipulation: base-rate use rose when random sampling could be watched rather than asserted. Kahneman and Tversky replied that the critique misrepresents their position, and that judgments of frequency carry large and systematic biases of their own. The second error is treating natural frequencies as a general fix. Weber, Binder and Krauss found that about 49% of people handed a frequency version converted it back into probabilities and calculated with those, and three-quarters still got it wrong. Chapman and Liu gave 346 students the Lipkus numeracy scale and split them at the median. On the medical scenario, correct answers went from 1% to 27% with frequencies among high scorers and from 0% to 7% among low scorers, a format-by-numeracy interaction of χ²(1) = 13.29, p = .0003. Bramwell's data point the same way: the format gain was statistically reliable only among obstetricians, who went from 1 of 21 correct with percentages to 13 of 20 with frequencies, while midwives got none right in either arm. The reformulation helps the people who could already have done the arithmetic. The third error is reading the medical result as a fact about doctors. Obstetricians were the best of Bramwell's four groups at 34%, ahead of companions at 15% and pregnant women at 9%, which says more about the question than about the professions. The courtroom version of the same mistake has its own name. Thompson and Schumann called it the prosecutor's fallacy: treating the chance of a forensic match given innocence as the chance of innocence given a match. In their first experiment 144 undergraduates read a case where 2% of people would match the defendant's hair. Told the figure as a conditional probability, 22.2% reasoned that way, against 4.2% told it as a percentage and a headcount, and mean judgments of guilt were .72 against .53. In a second experiment 73 students read one fallacious argument from each side; 68.5% called the defence argument correct, 28.8% the prosecution argument, and only 22.2% spotted both errors.
